paragraphs.source_en: Elephants, which are depicted in several sites, are a good indicator of climate as individuals require about 150 litres of water per day. However, they are also able to adapt to a drier environment as they can dig holes to find underground water supplies. Although depicted in only a few sites, rhinoceros also indicates a humid environment; when the weather is hot, rhinos drink water daily and therefore must remain close to water. In cooler temperatures they can go without drinking for several days if their food is moist. The presence of giraffe does not indicate wet environmental conditions as they are able to survive for long periods without water if their food is moist. Indeed, images of giraffe are still present in the Pastoral and Cabaline rock art, when the Central Sahara was considerably more arid than in the Early Holocene.

paragraphs.source_en: The best climatic indicator appears to be hippopotamuses. Although they are represented very rarely in the Round Head art and not always recognisable with certainty, their occurrence testifies to their existence in this region. The presence of hippopotamuses as a climatic-chronological indicator has been studied by Hallier and Hallier (2009). Based on the fact that hippos need permanent water throughout the year and cannot live in a region with alternating rainy and dry seasons, these authors suggest that hippopotamuses are associated with the abundant precipitations that occurred in the Central Sahara until the 9th millennium BP. They probably did not return to the study area after the dry episode at around 8,000–7,000 BP (Hallier & Hallier 2009).

paragraphs.source_en: This hypothesis is supported by Thomas (1977) who claims that hippopotamuses disappeared from the Erg Tihodaine, next to the Tassili, after the Epipalaeolithic period. However, an image of a hippopotamus of the Pastoral style has been found at Uan Muhuggiag in the Acacus (Mori 1964) and a supporter of the low chronology, Le Quellec (2006b), points out that hippopotamus bones are frequent in the Ténéré region at around 3,500–2,000 BP, a date which probably indicates the last possible survival period for this species in the Sahara. This is quite surprising in a period of increasing aridity in most Saharan regions, however, some water courses in the Central Saharan mountains may have still been active in providing water to the southern part of the Sahara.
